title: Dyna-Mind: Teaching Agents to Simulate
one_liner: Teach language-model agents to mentally preview multiple futures before acting, then strengthen that ability with feedback from real rollouts.
lead: AI agents are good at narrow tasks like math problems but fail at complex interactive tasks such as navigating a website or controlling a phone. The missing piece is the ability to mentally play out different actions and see where each leads before committing — what humans call vicarious trial and error. Dyna-Mind teaches agents this skill in two stages: first by showing them reasoning traces built from expanded search trees gathered from real environment interactions, then by reinforcing their simulation ability with feedback signals from actual outcomes.

problem.h2: Agents reason narrowly and cannot plan ahead
paras: Today's language-model agents (models that read a situation and write an action, like a browser controller or phone-use AI) work well when the answer is close and visible. Math problems, coding questions, fact lookups — these the agent can reason through in one or two steps. But interactive tasks like web navigation or computer control require many steps, and the agent must anticipate what will happen after each action to choose wisely.

A beginner tries to train the agent purely from examples: show it successful paths through web forms, phone screens, or game boards, and it learns to imitate. The problem: the agent has no internal model of how the world responds. It cannot preview consequences. When it reaches a situation not in the training examples, it guesses blindly instead of thinking ahead.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Teach the agent to construct and reason about branching futures during planning, then strengthen that simulation ability by training on both final outcomes and intermediate states from real rollouts.

steps.text: Gather real environment interactions and expand them into search trees, then write out the full reasoning that ties the tree to an action choice.
Show the agent reasoning traces and teach it to generate that same structured simulation-based reasoning directly, without needing the search algorithm.

steps.b: Stage 2: Collect rollouts and real outcomes
steps.text: Run the trained agent in the environment and record both what happens (the final success or failure) and the intermediate states it passes through.

steps.b: Stage 2: Train with outcome and state signals
steps.text: Use reinforcement learning to nudge the agent's reasoning and action-choosing, rewarding it when the simulated futures match what actually happened.

The agent can now mentally branch futures, and its simulations grow more accurate through real-world feedback, because each real rollout shows exactly where predictions diverged from reality and the reinforcement learning stage uses that difference to tune the model.

paras: The paper teaches a language model to write out its reasoning as a sequence of simulated future states, then picks actions that lead toward desired outcomes. This reasoning is explicit text, generated by the model itself during planning.

hidden.h2: The simulation fidelity — how well the agent's predictions match reality
hidden.name: simulation fidelity: how far ahead the agent can forecast accurately
paras: A language-model agent reasons by predicting the next state after each action. Simulation fidelity is how accurate those predictions are — does the agent correctly anticipate what the screen will look like after it clicks a button, or after it fills a form field? Higher fidelity means the agent's mental preview aligns with real outcomes.

The paper measures this implicitly: it trains the agent on reasoning traces built from real search trees (so the predictions come from genuine consequences), then tunes the model using reinforcement learning signals from actual rollouts. As the model improves, its predictions get more faithful to how the world actually responds, because the reinforcement learning stage explicitly penalizes predictions that do not match observed outcomes and rewards predictions that align with real states.

heat.caption: Darker means agent's prediction matched the real outcome. Highlights mark decision points where accuracy mattered.

reads.html: Imagine you are planning a route through a maze by picturing each turn in your head. If your mental picture is accurate, you will not hit dead ends. If your predictions are wrong, you will take false turns. Simulation fidelity is how clear and correct your mental picture is.

The paper trains agents to generate structured reasoning traces that include explicit future state predictions from expanded search trees built from real environment interactions. Stage 1 (ReSim) teaches the agent to output this reasoning directly. Stage 2 (Dyna-GRPO) refines the agent's predictions by comparing them against actual rollout outcomes and intermediate observed states.

paras: An agent that can only imitate past examples is blind to consequences. But if the agent can predict future states, it can reason about which action is likely to lead to the goal. The mechanism works in two parts.

First, Reasoning with Simulations (ReSim) anchors predictions to real futures. Instead of guessing what will happen, the algorithm builds a search tree by trying multiple actions in the real environment, then asks the language model to synthesize that whole tree into a single reasoning response that explains how the best path leads to success. Training on these responses teaches the model the relationship: if you take action A, then action B, then action C, the world state evolves this way and you reach the goal. The model learns not just imitation but causal structure.

Second, Dyna-GRPO strengthens those predictions with reinforcement learning feedback. When the agent generates actions in real rollouts, the algorithm observes both the final outcome (success or failure) and the intermediate states along the way. It then trains the agent to predict those intermediate states and choose actions that move through predicted high-value states. Because the predictions are grounded in real outcomes, the agent's simulations become more faithful and its planning more accurate.

stages.s: Observation (web form, phone screen, game board)
Agent scores each simulated path by predicted value
Agent picks action leading to highest-value simulated state
Action (click, type, scroll) executed in real environment

math.h2: Training loss that grounds simulation in real outcomes
math.words: The loss combines imitation learning (match the agent's reasoning to demonstration traces) and reinforcement learning (reward simulations that lead to high-value real outcomes).
symbols: loss from comparing agent's reasoning trace to the demonstration trace built from search tree
reinforcement learning loss that rewards actions leading to real task success
weight controlling how much to prioritize RL refinement over imitation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Agent reasoning: 'From state S, if I click button X, I will see form. Then if I type name, screen shows confirmation. Best path is X then type.'
Demonstration from search tree: 'From state S, action X leads to form (real outcome). Action type leads to confirmation (real outcome). This path succeeds.'
Imitation loss: difference between agent's prediction and observed outcome is 0.5 (agent predicted wrong details). L_imitation = 0.5.
Real rollout: agent takes the action sequence, reaches success. Reward = +1.0. L_RL = 0 (no penalty, because outcome was correct).
L_total = 0.5 + 0.1 * 0 = 0.5. On the next attempt, agent learns to refine its simulation.

math.note: The two losses pull together: imitation grounds the agent in real-world cause and effect, and reinforcement learning refines the predictions to match actual outcomes.

charts.title: Imitation-only baseline (memorizes patterns)
charts.note: Without internal simulation, the agent succeeds only on familiar cases and fails on unfamiliar situations or tasks requiring many steps.

charts.title: Dyna-Mind (with learned simulation)
charts.note: With simulation ability trained via ReSim and Dyna-GRPO, the agent reasons about new situations and handles long-horizon tasks. Success improves especially on unseen cases where the agent must mentally branch, because simulation-based reasoning generalizes better than memorized patterns — the agent can apply the same causal logic (action A leads to state B) to situations it has never seen before.

items.b: Simulation gets out of sync with reality.
items.html: If the agent's predictions drift away from how the world actually responds (e.g., it thinks clicking button A opens menu, but it opens a modal), planning will lead to wrong actions. The model needs constant feedback from real rollouts to recalibrate.

Building reasoning traces requires running multiple rollouts from each state to construct the search tree. This is much more costly than simple imitation. If environment interaction is expensive (e.g., interacting with a real website), collecting enough data becomes prohibitive.

items.b: Agent hallucinates plausible but false futures.
items.html: A language model can always generate text that sounds reasonable. If the training data has gaps or the model has poor inductive bias, it may predict futures that sound coherent but do not match the real environment, leading to planning failures.

items.b: Done right: simulation grounded in real outcomes.
items.html: When the training data comes from genuine environment interactions (not synthetic or hallucinated) and the reinforcement learning stage continuously updates predictions against real feedback, the agent's simulation becomes trustworthy and planning improves, because the model learns the true causal structure of the world rather than plausible-sounding but false patterns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo should show that an agent trained with Dyna-Mind can solve a multi-step task by reasoning about futures. Use a simple grid world (like Sokoban: push a box to a goal in a small room) or a text-based task (like a form-filling chain). Train two versions: one with imitation-only, one with Dyna-Mind (ReSim + Dyna-GRPO). The key test is to give both agents a puzzle they have never seen during training (a different room layout or form structure). The imitation-only agent should fail or choose suboptimal actions because it cannot reason ahead. The Dyna-Mind agent should branch futures mentally, predict which action leads closer to the goal, and solve the task. Measure success rate and average number of steps to completion.
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that only when the agent simulates futures does it solve unfamiliar multi-step tasks reliably.
